Guatavita, a mountain lake near Bogotá, is one of the best-known places associated with the legend of El Dorado. It was sacred to the Muisca people. According to the account of a ruler's inauguration, the chief went out onto the water on a raft while participants in the ceremony lowered gold objects into the lake.

The story of the ritual later drew treasure hunters and expeditions to the site. Today, a visit to the lake combines an introduction to pre-Columbian culture with a walk along mountain trails. From the shores, there are views of the water and surrounding slopes. A visit to Guatavita is often combined with Zipaquirá on a trip from Bogotá.

The vast waters of Lake Maracaibo lie in western Venezuela. Its southwestern section is associated with humid coastal landscapes and the Catatumbo area. Water, river channels and vegetation along the banks form a natural setting best explored on a boat trip.

The area is known for Catatumbo lightning, which visitors come to observe on nighttime excursions. By day, birds, howler monkeys and iguanas attract attention; after dark, other inhabitants of the coastal wetlands can be observed. Exploring Maracaibo reveals Venezuela's aquatic and marshland environments, complementing the country's mountain and coastal routes.

Lake Nicaragua is known for the country's waterscapes and island excursions from Granada. Boat routes pass between green islands, where the water and shoreline vegetation create a distinct natural setting. Views of Mombacho Volcano open up in this area.

Exploring the lake complements a visit to the colonial city. From the water, you see a different side of Granada's surroundings, with islands and small piers. Trips to Zopango and other parts of the lake offer time to enjoy this scenery. The lake connects city itineraries with Nicaragua's natural and volcanic geography.
